title: The Mobilisation Gap: Why Your Biggest Win of the Year Can Be Your Tightest Month of Cash
excerpt: Winning the biggest contract of the year feels like the turning point every owner is chasing. For many East Coast businesses, it is also the moment cash gets tightest, weeks before the new revenue ever lands.
content:
There is a particular kind of good news that lands on an owner's desk this time of year: the client who has been circling for months finally signs, the tender comes back won, the order is bigger than anyone expected. It is the kind of moment that gets celebrated around the office, and it should be. Then, three or four weeks later, the bank balance looks tighter than it did before the win, and nobody quite understands why.

The pattern is common enough across East Coast businesses heading into the spring trading lift that it is worth naming properly. A big contract does not arrive with its own cash attached. It arrives with a bill, usually before a single dollar of the new revenue has landed.

This is not a sign that the business made a bad decision. It is a timing mechanism that catches profitable, well-run businesses more often than it catches struggling ones, because the businesses doing the winning are usually the ones growing fastest.

Why the Celebration Comes Before the Cash

Every new contract of any size carries a mobilisation period, the stretch between saying yes and the first invoice actually being paid. During that stretch, the costs show up immediately and in full. Staff get hired or redeployed, stock or raw materials get ordered to the new specification, equipment gets bought or hired, sometimes a bond or bank guarantee has to be posted before work can even start. None of that waits for a payment schedule. A contract that requires three extra staff has them on the payroll from week one, while the client being served may not release a single payment until the end of the first full billing cycle.

The revenue, by contrast, moves at the pace of the contract terms, not the pace of the costs. Milestone billing, 30 to 60 day payment terms, a probation period before the client commits to full volume, all of it means the cash coming in lags well behind the cash already spent. On paper, in the profit and loss, the contract looks exactly as good as it is. In the bank account, for a window that can run eight to twelve weeks, it looks like the opposite.

Why the Biggest Wins Create the Biggest Gaps

The size of the contract makes the timing problem worse, not better, and that is the part most owners do not see coming. A client worth an extra ten percent of current revenue creates a mobilisation cost that is manageable against the existing cash base. A client worth fifty or a hundred percent of current revenue creates a mobilisation cost on a completely different scale, funded by a business that was never sized for it. The business has not changed how it operates. It has simply taken on a cash commitment several multiples larger than any it has carried before, while its buffer is still sized for the business it was last quarter.

It is the reason the biggest win of the year is so often also the tightest quarter of the year. The business did everything right. It won the work it was chasing. The gap is purely mechanical, and it catches businesses that have never had reason to think about it before, because every previous contract they have won was small enough for the existing buffer to absorb.

Modelling the Gap Before You Say Yes, Not After

The fix is not to turn down good contracts. It is to model the mobilisation period before signing, not three weeks into it. A rolling 13-Week Cash Flow Build built around the specific shape of the new contract, not the business as a whole, shows exactly which week the gap opens and how wide it gets before the first payment arrives. That single piece of visibility changes the conversation from why is the account so tight to we knew this week was coming and we are funded for it.

Often the funding does not need to come from outside the business at all. A Working Capital Unlock review frequently finds enough cash already trapped in existing debtors, inventory or supplier terms to self-fund a mobilisation period that looks, from the outside, like it needs an overdraft increase. Businesses that build this kind of cash flow discipline into how they evaluate new work, rather than discovering the gap after the contract has started, tend to take on growth at a pace the business can actually carry.

None of this is a reason to hesitate on the next big opportunity. It is a reason to ask one extra question before accepting it, not whether the contract is profitable, which it almost certainly is, but whether the business can fund the weeks before that profit becomes cash. For many owner-led businesses across Queensland and the broader East Coast heading into the final quarter of the year, that is the question a fractional CFO conversation is built to answer before the contract is signed, not after.

faqs.q: Why does cash flow feel tighter right after winning a big new contract?
faqs.a: A new contract carries a mobilisation period, the gap between saying yes and the first payment landing. Costs like staff, stock and equipment show up immediately, while revenue follows the contract's own payment terms, which usually lag weeks behind. Building that pattern into day-to-day cash flow discipline stops it from feeling like a surprise.

faqs.q: What is a mobilisation period in the context of a new business contract?
faqs.a: It is the stretch of time between a contract being signed and the business actually receiving its first payment under that contract. Costs to deliver the work, staffing, stock, equipment and sometimes bonds or guarantees, start immediately, while the revenue follows the slower rhythm of invoicing terms and milestone billing.

faqs.q: How much working capital should a business set aside before a large contract starts?
faqs.a: There is no fixed figure, since it depends on the scale of the new work relative to current revenue and how quickly costs need to be paid versus when the client pays. A Working Capital Unlock review maps exactly how much cash a specific contract will consume before it returns a dollar.

faqs.q: Should a profitable contract ever be delayed because of cash flow timing?
faqs.a: Rarely does it need to be turned down outright, but the start date, staged delivery or payment terms are often worth renegotiating once the mobilisation gap is understood. A contract that is genuinely profitable on paper can still strain a business that has not planned for the weeks before that profit turns into cash.

faqs.q: How can a 13-week cash flow forecast help before accepting a new client?
faqs.a: A forecast built around the specific shape of the new contract shows which week the cash gap opens and how wide it becomes before the first payment arrives. That visibility turns a stressful surprise into a funded, expected dip, which is the core purpose of a fractional CFO engagement during a growth phase.

faqs.q: Do East Coast SMEs typically fund this gap with a bank facility or existing cash?
faqs.a: Both are used, but many businesses across Queensland and the broader East Coast already have enough cash trapped in debtors, inventory or supplier terms to self-fund a mobilisation period without increasing debt. Finding that cash first is usually cheaper and faster than arranging new finance under time pressure.
